B.1 Machining and inspection The quality of the RF surfaces has a tremendous effect on the high gradient performance of an NCRF accelerating construction. Precise mating surfaces and registrations features are also critically important since these determine the alignment between the RF quads as well as the final straightness of the AS. Precision machine tools, RF-specific machining expertise and state-of-the-art computer aided manufacturing(CAM) software are critical to achieving these requirements. B.1.1 Feedstock material considerations The properties of the feedstock material have a significant effect on the quality of the finished part. The materials standard for high power RF devices is ASTM F68: Standard Specification for Oxygen-Free Copper in Wrought Forms for Electron Devices, which contains specifications for chemical purity, surface defects, sub-surface microporosity, grain size as well hydrogen embrittlement testing. A key requirement of F68-grade copper is low oxygen content, with a maximum 5 ppm of O permitted. This would be considered Oxygen Free Electronic grade copper. Furthermore, most accelerator applications additionally require the use of F68 Class 2 or better copper, which is determined through special macro and microscopic investigation. During the development of the CLIC AS technology, CERN established standard for high gradient copper, EDMS No: 790779: Oxygen-Free Electronic copper Bars/blanks/ingots. This standard further builds upon ASTM F68 by including specifications for multi-directional 3D forging, half-hard temper (yield strength: 200- 240 MPa minimum, tensile strength: 240-280 MPa) and fine (max. 90 μm) and homogeneous grain size (ASTM E112, grain size 4 or greater). Including requirements on forging and temper limits risks of voids during machining. The homogeneity of the material is 100% ultrasonically inspected to detect any potential continuity faults, following CERN specifications [13]. One fundamental challenge concerning precision manufacturing of welded accelerating structures is the internal residual stress within the stock material. Cold work process such as rolling or forging hardens copper by creating residual compressive and tensile stress throughout the material.
